planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container divisions in spring into sharply drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Magic Carpet knits into a solid flowering mat within a season and is one of the more reliably floriferous creeping thyme selections.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery divisions into sharply drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun. Magic Carpet forms an exceptionally dense, low mat of tiny gray-green leaves that all but disappears under a heavy midsummer flush of lavender-pink flowers, one of the showiest and most uniform bloom displays among the creeping thymes and a strong pollinator draw. It tolerates light foot traffic once established, releasing a faint aromatic scent when brushed or stepped on, making it a favorite filler between flagstones and pavers and along the edges of gravel paths. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tight and encourage a fuller second flush; avoid heavy, poorly drained soils where the shallow roots are prone to rot.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in spring into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; Reiter's Red is noted for holding up especially well to heat, aridity, and reflected sun from stone and gravel, making it a favorite of high-desert and xeric plantings.

directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container-grown starts in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun. Reiter's Red forms a very low, wiry mat of small dark green leaves topped with a dense, deep rose-red flower display in early summer that reads redder than most other creeping thyme cultivars, and it has a reputation among xeriscape growers for outperforming other red-flowered thymes in hot, dry, high-altitude conditions. It tolerates light foot traffic once established and is a good choice for gravel gardens, dry stone paths, and the gaps between flagstones in full-sun sites where many other groundcovers struggle. Shear lightly right after bloom to maintain a tight mat and prevent the center from opening up and going woody; avoid rich or consistently damp soil.
sources: Plant Select (Colorado State University / Denver Botanic Gardens)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring into moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; the white-flowered form spreads and knits together at the same steady pace as the species and tolerates the same light foot traffic.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun where summers are mild. 'Alba' is the white-flowered form of creeping mazus, forming the same tight, ground-hugging mat of small bright green leaves as the species but studded with small pure-white, snapdragon-like flowers in late spring rather than the typical lavender-blue, giving a cooler, brighter effect between pavers and stepping stones. It spreads readily by rooting at the nodes to close gaps within a season or two and tolerates light, occasional foot traffic once established. Keep soil evenly moist through summer, since the shallow roots dry out quickly in hot, exposed sites, and divide congested patches in spring to renew vigor or start new plantings.

planting.note: Set out small starter plugs or divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; the dark bronze-black foliage colors up most intensely with some direct sun exposure, unlike the plain green species which prefers more shade.

directions: Plant divisions or starter plugs in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Platt's Black is a striking selection of brass buttons with finely divided, fern-like foliage in a deep bronze to near-black color that darkens further with more sun exposure, creating a dramatic textural and color contrast against green lawns, gravel, and lighter-colored pavers where it is often used as an accent ribbon along path edges. Like the species it spreads by creeping rhizomes into a dense, low carpet, tolerates light foot traffic once established, and bears small inconspicuous yellow-green button flowers in summer that are secondary to the foliage color. Keep soil from drying out for extended periods and divide congested patches in spring to fill bare spots or start new plantings.

planting.note: Set out small starter plugs or divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Scotch moss needs consistent moisture to hold its bright golden color and knit into a solid mat, and struggles through hot, humid summers the same way the green species does.

directions: Plant small starter plugs into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. 'Aurea' is the golden-foliaged form of Sagina subulata, forming the same tight, moss-like mat as the green species but in a bright chartreuse-gold color that glows underfoot and makes a vivid contrast planted alongside darker stone, green turf, or bronze-leaved companions, with small white star-shaped flowers appearing in early summer. It tolerates light foot traffic once the mat has filled in and is a popular choice for edging paver joints and stepping-stone paths in cool-summer climates, but it needs consistent moisture and struggles in hot, humid, or drought-prone conditions where the color bleaches and the mat can thin out. Water regularly during dry spells and avoid walking on newly set plugs until they root in.
